analysis.one_liner: Redirects federal mine-reclamation money to shore up pensions for retired coal miners and widows.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 111 bipartisan cosponsors and cleared a House committee markup in October 2019, but no chamber ever voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2021; its central pension transfer was enacted separately in a December 2019 spending bill.
analysis.plain_summary: The 1974 United Mine Workers of America Pension Plan — which pays promised pensions to retired coal miners and their widows — was running out of money because coal companies that went bankrupt or withdrew stopped paying into it. This bill would have Treasury divert any money in the Abandoned Mine Reclamation Fund above what's needed for current reclamation obligations into the pension plan, and raise the annual cap on transfers from that fund from $490 million to $750 million. Transfers would stop once the plan was fully funded, benefit increases would be barred while money was flowing in, and the plan's trustees would have to file detailed annual reports to Treasury and the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation. A separate section would let people take money out of their own pension plans while still working at age 59½ instead of 62.
analysis.who_benefits: Retired coal miners and surviving spouses in the 1974 UMWA Pension Plan, whose promised pensions were endangered when coal companies went bankrupt and stopped contributing. Active miners' families also benefit because their future pensions sit in the same plan.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retired coal miners and their widows

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Treasury Department to transfer any Abandoned Mine Reclamation Fund money above existing reclamation obligations to the 1974 UMWA Pension Plan to pay required pension benefits.
Raises the annual cap on transfers from the reclamation fund from $490 million to $750 million, enlarging the pool of money available for the pension plan.

Includes safeguards: transfers cease once the plan is 100 percent funded, no plan amendments can increase benefits or liabilities while transfers flow, and trustees must file enhanced annual reports with Treasury and the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation.

analysis.who_pays: The Abandoned Mine Reclamation Fund — money raised from fees on coal production — would have less left over for reclaiming abandoned mine sites. Coal operators that had stopped contributing would face no new obligation to pay the shortfall themselves.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mine-reclamation funding; coal companies pay nothing new

drawbacks.text: The transfers stop once the plan reaches 100 percent funding, but the underlying problem — a shrinking base of active coal miners contributing as the industry contracts — is not fixed, so the plan could fall back into shortfall later.
Money directed to pensions is money not available for the fund's original purpose of reclaiming abandoned and hazardous mine sites.

The bill attaches an unrelated retirement change: it lowers the minimum age for taking in-service distributions from a pension or governmental 457(b) plan from 62 to 59½ for all plans, not just miners' pensions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is a good one for working people: promised retirement benefits to miners and widows get paid with surplus reclamation-fee money rather than general tax dollars, at a modest cost to mine-land cleanup. But the design is a stopgap — it fills the plan without requiring the coal companies that created the shortfall to contribute, and it does nothing about the shrinking contributor base, so the fix could need renewing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared a House subcommittee and was approved in committee by voice vote in October 2019, but it was never scheduled for a vote on the House or Senate floor and died when the Congress ended in January 2021 — though Congress separately enacted its central pension transfer that December in a spending bill.

narrative.text: Introduced on January 31, 2019 by Rep. David McKinley (R-WV), the bill was referred to the Natural Resources and Ways and Means Committees.
It drew 111 cosponsors — 89 of 231 House Democrats and 22 of 197 House Republicans.

A House Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee held a hearing on July 24, 2019, and on October 23, 2019 the Natural Resources Committee discharged the subcommittee, held a markup, and ordered the bill reported (amended) by voice vote.
No further action was ever recorded: the bill never received a vote on the House floor or in the Senate, and the 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021.

In December 2019, Congress enacted the Bipartisan American Miners Act as part of a government funding package, adopting the core idea of this bill by directing up to $750 million a year from the Abandoned Mine Reclamation Fund to the 1974 UMWA Pension Plan.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Retired miners and widows came out ahead in substance: the pension transfer they needed was enacted through a December 2019 spending bill even though this bill itself died without a vote, and coal operators avoided any new requirement to fund the plan.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Retired miners, whose fix passed anyway

sides.party_line_note: Support crossed party lines: 89 of 231 House Democrats and 22 of 197 House Republicans cosponsored, and the committee approved it on a voice vote with no recorded opposition.

industries.note: Coal operators that went bankrupt or withdrew from the plan stopped paying into it, creating the shortfall. The bill pays the promised pensions from a federal fund without requiring those companies to contribute anything, so their legacy pension obligations get covered at no cost to them.

industries.industry: United Mine Workers of America (1974 Pension Plan)
industries.note: The union-run plan receives federal transfers that let it pay promised benefits to retirees and widows rather than cut them.

Surplus money in the reclamation fund that could go toward cleaning up abandoned and hazardous mine sites is redirected to pensions instead — a real but modest cost borne partly by communities near old mines.
